---
title: 1.1 Rates of Change and Limits
subtitle: Limits from Graphs
output: pdf_document
---

1. For the function $g(x)$ graphed here, find the following limits or explain
   why they do not exist.

```{r exercise_1, out.width="55%", fig.align = "center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/01-Chapter/01-01-p01.png")
```

Each of the limits is found by observation.

> a. $\lim_{x\to 1} g(x)$

The limit does not exist. From the left $\lim_{x\to 1^-} g(x) = 1$, and from
the right, $\lim_{x\to 1^+} g(x) = 0$. Since the one-sided limits are
different, $\lim_{x\to 1} g(x)$ does not exist.

> b. $\lim_{x \to 2} g(x)$

The limit does exist and equals $1$.

> c. $\lim_{x \to 3} g(x)$

The limit exists and equals $0$. The open circle at $(3, 0)$ shows that $g(3)
\ne 0$, but the limit depends only on the values of $g(x)$ near $x = 3$, not
$g(3)$ itself.

---

2. For the function $g(t)$ graphed here, find the following limits or explain
   why they do not exist.

```{r exercise_2, out.width="55%", fig.align = "center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/01-Chapter/01-01-p02.png")
```

>  a. $\lim_{t \to -2} g(t)$

The limit exists and equals $0$. The open circle at $(-2, 0)$ shows that $g(-2)
\ne 0$, but the values of $g(t)$ approach $0$.

>  b. $\lim_{t \to -1} g(t)$

The limit exists and is $-1$.

>  c. $\lim_{t \to 0} g(t)$

The limit does not exist. From the left, $\lim_{t\to 0^-} g(t) = -1$, and from
the right, $\lim_{t\to 0^+} g(t) = 1$. Since the one-sided limits are
different, $\lim_{t\to 0} g(t)$ does not exist, even though $g(0) = 0$ is
defined.

---

3. Which of the following statements about the function $y = f(x)$ graphed here
   are true, and which are false?

```{r exercise_3, out.width="55%", fig.align = "center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/01-Chapter/01-01-p03.png")
```

> a. $\lim_{x\to0} f(x)$ exists

This statement is true. $\lim_{x\to0} f(x) = 0$ even though $f(0) = 1$ is
defined.

> b. $\lim_{x\to0} f(x) = 0$

This is true. Both one-sided limits $\lim_{x\to0^-} f(x)$ and $\lim_{x\to0^+}
f(x)$ equal $0$.

> c. $\lim_{x\to0} f(x) = 1$

This is false. $f(0) = 1$ is defined, but $\lim_{x\to0} f(x) = 0$.

> d. $\lim_{x\to1} f(x) = 1$

This is false. $\lim_{x\to1^-} f(x) = -1$ and $\lim_{x\to1^+} f(x) = 0$, so the
one-sided limits are different and the limit does not exist.

> e. $\lim_{x\to1} f(x) = 0$

This is false. Even though $f(1) = 0$, the limit does not exist for the same
reason as in (d).

> f. $\lim_{x\to x_0} f(x)$ exists at every point $x_0$ in $(-1, 1)$.

This is true. At every $x_0 \ne 0$ in $(-1, 1)$, the graph is an unbroken line
near $x_0$, so the limit exists. At $x_0 = 0$, both one-sided limits equal $0$,
so the limit exists there too, even though $f(0) = 1$ and $f$ is not continuous
at $0$.

---

4. Which of the following statements about the function $y = f(x)$ graphed here
   are true, and which are false?

```{r exercise_4, out.width="55%", fig.align = "center", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("../../figures/01-Chapter/01-01-p04.png")
```

> a. $\lim_{x\to2} f(x)$ does not exist.

This is false. Both one-sided limits equal $1$, so the limit exists.

> b. $\lim_{x\to2} f(x) = 2$

This is false. The limit is $1$, not $2$.

> c. $\lim_{x\to1} f(x)$ does not exist.

This is true. Approaching from the left, $\lim_{x\to1^-} f(x) = -2$ and
approaching from the right, $\lim_{x\to1^+} f(x) = 0$. The one-sided limits are
different and therefore the limit does not exist. Note that $f(1) = 0$, but the
value at $x = 1$ does not affect the limit.

> d. $\lim_{x\to x_0} f(x)$ exists at every point $x_0$ in $(-1, 1)$.

This is true. The graph is unbroken across $(-1, 1)$. At the corner at $x = 0$,
both one-sided limits equal $0$, so the limit exists there as well.

> e. $\lim_{x\to x_0} f(x)$ exists at every point $x_0$ in $(1, 3)$.

This is true. On $(1, 3)$ the graph is unbroken except at $x = 2$, where the
value $f(2) = 0$ lies off the curve. Since $\lim_{x\to 2^-} f(x) = 1$ and
$\lim_{x\to 2^+} f(x) = 1$, the limit exists at $x = 2$ as well.
